title: পুরুষ
Purush
Person & pronouns
blurb: Who is speaking, who is spoken to, who is spoken about: the three persons, the three levels of 'you', and every pronoun form.

blocks.text: পুরুষ (purush) means 'person' in the grammatical sense. Every sentence has a doer, and the doer is always one of three kinds: the person who is speaking, the person who is being spoken to, or somebody or something else who is being spoken about. Bengali verbs change their ending to match this person, so the very first thing to learn is which person you are talking about.
Some books call the third person প্রথম পুরুষ (first person, counting in the Sanskrit order). Ask your teacher which labels your class uses.
The same sentence in all three persons
Look at one action, 'goes to school', with each person. Only the pronoun and the verb ending change: the rest of the sentence stays the same.
The verb does not change for number

English changes the verb for number sometimes ('he goes', 'they go'). Bengali does not. The pronoun already carries the number (আমি or আমরা, সে or তারা); the verb stays exactly the same as in the singular. So সে যায় (he goes) and তারা যায় (they go) use the same verb form, and so do আমি যাই and আমরা যাই.

blocks.title: Singular and plural take the same verb
items: You all (respectful) go to the office.
He / she goes to the park.

blocks.title: No gender in Bengali pronouns or verbs
blocks.text: সে means both 'he' and 'she'; তিনি means both 'he' and 'she' (respectful). Nothing in the verb tells you whether the doer is male or female. In English you are forced to choose, so when you translate সে যায় you must pick 'he' or 'she' from the situation.
items: He goes to school. / She goes to school.
He goes to the office. / She goes to the office.

blocks.text: English has one word, 'you'. Bengali has three: তুই, তুমি and আপনি. They are not different words for different numbers, they are different levels of respect, and each one needs its own verb ending. Choosing the right level is the most important social skill in Bengali, because the wrong choice can sound rude or can sound cold.

blocks.title: Which one should I use?
items: Use আপনি with anyone you do not know, anyone older than you, and anyone in a formal setting: a shop, an office, a hospital, a classroom with a new teacher.
Use তুমি with friends, classmates, people of your own age who have been friendly, and children you are not close to.
Use তুই only with people who are very close to you, and only when you are sure. In some families and friendships it is normal, in others it is rude.
Teachers often say তুমি to students and students say আপনি to teachers. Customs differ between families, so listen to how people address each other and follow them.
If you are not sure, use আপনি. It is never rude. The other person will usually tell you to use তুমি.

blocks.title: Do not mix the levels
items: আপনি always takes the -েন ending. যাচ্ছ belongs to তুমি.
তুমি takes -ছ. The -ছেন ending is for আপনি and তিনি.

sections.title: He, she, it, they: the third person

blocks.text: The third person is everyone and everything that is not the speaker and not the listener. Like 'you', the third person has an ordinary form and a respectful form. The respectful form takes the same verb ending as আপনি.
Ordinary and respectful in sentences

blocks.title: Pairs: ordinary and respectful
items: That one listens to a song.
That person (respected) listens to a song.

blocks.text: Names and nouns behave the same way

When the doer is a noun instead of a pronoun, the same rule applies. Respected people (parents, teachers, doctors, elders) take the respectful verb ending, as if you had said তিনি. Friends, children, animals and objects take the ordinary ending, as if you had said সে.

blocks.title: Respected people and others
items: The doctor stays at the hospital.

blocks.text: It is a matter of respect, not of age alone. Calling a younger doctor or a teacher by the respectful form is correct. In a close family, some people use the ordinary form for an older brother or sister. Follow what your own family does.

blocks.title: Match the verb to the level
items: সে is the ordinary pronoun, so the verb is যায়. Use তিনি যান for the respectful form.
তিনি is respectful, so the verb ends in -েন.
A mother takes the respectful verb. খায় sounds as if you called her সে.

blocks.text: A pronoun changes its shape depending on the job it does in the sentence. As the doer (subject) it is আমি, তুমি, সে. As the receiver of the action (object) it takes -কে: আমাকে, তোমাকে, তাকে. To show ownership (possessive) it takes -র: আমার, তোমার, তার. In the plural, one form ending in -দের does both the object and the possessive job.
Object: who receives the action

blocks.title: Object forms in use
items: The teacher told us a story.

blocks.text: Possessive: whose is it?

blocks.title: Subject, object and possessive
items: The possessive comes before the thing owned: আমার বই, 'my book'.
The receiver of the action needs the object form আমাকে, not the subject form আমি.
For 'his / her' use the possessive তার, not the object form তাকে.

blocks.text: Pointing words go in front of a noun. Bengali has two for 'that': one for something you can see or point at (ওই), and one for something already mentioned (সেই). The question word 'which' is কোন, and the relative word 'who / which' is যে.
The little endings -টা and -টি after the noun (বইটা, বাড়িটা) mean 'the'. They are explained in the lesson on number and counting.
নিজে means 'by oneself, in person'. It stresses that the doer did it alone. নিজের means 'one's own'. Both can be added to any person.

blocks.title: Doing it yourself
items: I do my own work myself.
He / she cooks by himself / herself.

blocks.text: Because the verb ending already shows the person, Bengali very often leaves the pronoun out when it is clear who is meant. You will hear this constantly in speech. Keep the pronoun when you want to stress who is doing it, or when it would otherwise be unclear.

blocks.title: No pronoun needed
items: (Where are you going?)  The verb -ছ shows 'you' (তুমি).
(I am eating rice.)  The verb -ছি shows 'I'.
(I will go to the market.)  The ending -ব shows 'I'.
(What are you doing?)  The ending -ছেন shows আপনি.
(Will you have tea?)  The ending -বে with a question shows তুমি.

blocks.text: The ending -বে is the same for তুমি and সে (খাবে). When no pronoun is given, context tells you which one is meant.

title: ক্রিয়া
Kriya
Verbs
blurb: Roots and endings, finite and non-finite verbs, 'to be' and 'to have', commands and polite requests, verbs made with করা, and verbs that make others act.

blocks.text: The action word of a sentence is the ক্রিয়া (kriya). Every Bengali verb is built from a root, called ধাতু (dhatu). You add an ending to the root, and the ending tells you who is acting (the person) and when (the tense). To use a verb you need three things: the root, the ending, and the person.

blocks.title: How to find the root
blocks.text: The dictionary form of a verb is the verbal noun, which ends in -া: করা, বলা, খাওয়া, যাওয়া. To get the root, take off the -া (and the -ওয়া in verbs like খাওয়া, যাওয়া, দেওয়া).
More verbs: dictionary form and root

Some roots change their vowel when an ending is added: লেখা has the root লিখ- in লিখি (I write) but লেখো in 'you write'; শোনা gives শুনি and শোনো. This is called vowel harmony and you learn it with practice. The verb tables in the Tenses lessons always show the right forms.

A regular verb keeps its root the same and just takes the endings. করা, বলা, দেখা, পড়া, চলা, থাকা, বসা, খেলা and হাঁটা are regular. An irregular verb changes its root in some tenses. খাওয়া, যাওয়া, দেওয়া, নেওয়া and আসা are the most common irregular verbs, and you must memorise them.

A finite verb (সমাপিকা ক্রিয়া, shomapika kriya) ends a sentence and carries the person and the tense: আমি ভাত খাই। A non-finite verb (অসমাপিকা ক্রিয়া, oshomapika kriya) does not end a sentence by itself. It has no person and no tense of its own, and it hangs on to a finite verb that comes later in the sentence. There are four non-finite forms.

blocks.title: Four non-finite forms of nineteen common verbs
head: Verb
Root (ধাতু)
-ে / -য়ে (and then)
-তে (to do)
-লে (if)
-া (verbal noun)

blocks.text: 1. The -ে form: 'having done', 'and then'
Add -ে (or -য়ে after a vowel) to the root. It joins two actions that happen one after the other. The person and tense are shown only on the last verb.

blocks.title: -ে: one action after another
items: Having eaten rice, he / she went to school.
I went to the market and bought fish.
He / she read a book and fell asleep.
I opened the door and went inside.
He / she said with a smile, 'All right.'

blocks.text: 2. The -তে form: 'to do'
Add -তে to the root. It means 'in order to do' or 'to do', and it goes with verbs like চাই (want), পারি (can), হবে (must), এসেছি (have come).

blocks.title: -তে: to do something
items: I want to go to school.
He / she has gone to the market to buy fish.
I have come to see you.
He / she sat down to eat.
We will go for a walk tomorrow.

blocks.text: 3. The -লে form: 'if'
Add -লে to the root. It makes the 'if' part of a sentence. The main part of the sentence comes after it, usually in the future tense.

blocks.title: -লে: if
items: If you come, I will be happy.
If it rains, I will not go.
If you say so, I will do it.
If he / she studies, he / she will pass.
If you eat rice, you will get strength.
If I had known, I would have said so.

blocks.text: 4. The -া form: the verbal noun
The verbal noun names the action, like English 'reading' or 'to read' used as a thing. It can be the subject of a sentence, and it is the dictionary form of the verb.

blocks.title: -া: the action as a noun
items: Walking in the morning is good for health.
My reading of the book is finished.
Has the eating been done? (Have you eaten?)

blocks.title: Non-finite verbs need a finite verb
items: A non-finite verb cannot end the sentence. It needs a finite verb after it.
The root of যাওয়া changes: যা + তে becomes যেতে.

blocks.text: Bengali has no word for 'am / is / are' in the simple present when you say what someone or something is. You just put the two words together: আমি ছাত্র (I student) means 'I am a student'. But you do need a verb when you say that somebody or something is in a place or exists. That verb is আছে, a form of থাকা. The forms of আছ- cover the present; the past and the future use ছিল and থাকবে.
Where someone or something is

blocks.title: Place: আছে, ছিল, থাকবে
items: The book is on the table.
He / she is still at the office.
Tomorrow I will be at home.
When will you be at the office?

blocks.text: How someone is
Saying what someone is: no verb needed
When you name an identity or a quality, the present tense has no verb. The negative has its own forms: নই, নও, নন, নয়.

blocks.title: আছে or no verb?
items: Do not use আছি to say what you are. Use it only for place or existence.
For location you do need আছি.

blocks.text: Bengali has no verb 'to have'. To say that you have something, you say that it exists for you: 'of me a book is', আমার একটা বই আছে. The owner takes the possessive form (আমার, তোমার, তার…) and the verb is আছে. The negative is নেই ('there is not').

blocks.title: Having
items: How many brothers do you have?
I will have a holiday tomorrow.

blocks.text: কাছে ('near, with') is often added for things you carry or can use right now: আমার কাছে টাকা আছে means 'I have money on me'. আমার টাকা আছে means 'I have money' in general.

A command (অনুজ্ঞা) is the form of the verb you use to tell someone to do something. Like the pronouns, commands come at three levels, and the level you choose decides how polite you are. For তুই you use the bare root; for তুমি you add -ো (or -ও); for আপনি you add -ুন.
Giving instructions

blocks.title: Commands in use
items: Please give me a little water. (respectful)

blocks.text: Do not do it: negative commands

To forbid something, put না after the command with the normal তুমি or আপনি form. For তুই use the present form with -স and না. For আপনি you can also use the future form, which is more polite: আপনি করবেন না.
Polite requests with the future
A very polite way to ask for something is to use the future tense with আপনি as a question. It sounds like 'Will you …?'.

blocks.title: Requests with -বেন
items: Will you give me a little water?
Will you sit here for a moment?
Will you help me a little?
Will you speak a bit slowly?
Will you write your name for me?

sections.title: Verbs made with নাম + করা, হওয়া, পাওয়া

blocks.text: Many Bengali actions are said with a noun plus a helper verb. We do not say 'to work' with one verb. We say কাজ করা, 'to do work'. The helper verb carries the person and the tense; the noun carries the meaning. The helpers you meet most are করা (do), হওয়া (be, become), পাওয়া (get) and লাগা (feel, seem).
With করা
Feelings with পাওয়া and লাগা: the person is in the possessive

For feelings, Bengali says the feeling 'comes to' the person. The person takes the possessive form (আমার, তোমার, তার), not the subject form. So 'I am hungry' is আমার খিদে পেয়েছে, literally 'of me hunger has been got'.

blocks.title: Feeling

I think he / she will come.

blocks.text: Two verbs together
A verb in the -ে form can join a helper verb to add a shade of meaning: finished, completed, for oneself, suddenly. These helpers are common in speech.

sections.title: Making someone do it: the -ানো verbs

blocks.text: Add -ানো to a verb's root to make it mean 'make someone do it'. This is the causative form (প্রযোজক ক্রিয়া). খাওয়া 'to eat' becomes খাওয়ানো 'to feed'; পড়া 'to read' becomes পড়ানো 'to teach'; দেখা 'to see' becomes দেখানো 'to show'. The one who is made to act takes the ending -কে.

title: কাল
Kal
Tenses: the big picture
blurb: What a tense is, how every Bengali tense is built, the time words that go with each, and how to choose the right one.

blocks.text: কাল (kal) means 'time'. A tense tells us when an action happens: now, in the past, or in the future. Bengali has three times (বর্তমান, অতীত, ভবিষ্যৎ), and for each one it has kinds: simple (সাধারণ, a plain fact or habit), continuous (ঘটমান, still going on), and perfect (পুরাঘটিত, finished). The past also has a habitual kind (নিত্যবৃত্ত: 'used to'). That gives nine tenses.

blocks.title: One sentence in all nine tenses
head: Tense

blocks.title: Words you will meet
items: বর্তমান (bortoman) = present: now, and what is always true.
অতীত (otit) = past: it has already happened.
ভবিষ্যৎ (bhobishyot) = future: it has not happened yet.
সাধারণ (sadharon) = simple: a plain action, a habit or a fact.
ঘটমান (ghotoman) = continuous: the action is in progress.
পুরাঘটিত (puraghotito) = perfect: the action is complete.
নিত্যবৃত্ত (nityobritto) = habitual: it used to happen regularly.

blocks.text: Teachers and books use slightly different labels for some tenses. Check the names against your class notes. The forms themselves do not change.

Every tense is built the same way: root + tense sign + person ending. The root carries the meaning. The tense sign tells you when. The person ending tells you who. Once you know the signs, you can build any tense of any regular verb.

Notice the pattern. The continuous tenses use -ছ- (করছি) and the perfect tenses add an extra -ে (করেছি). Putting -ছিল- instead of -ছ- moves a tense into the past (করছি → করছিলাম; করেছি → করেছিলাম). The -ল- sign is the plain past, -ত- is the habitual past, and -ব- is the future.

sections.title: Time words and the tenses they go with

blocks.text: Time words are the quickest clue to the tense. When you hear রোজ (every day) you expect a habit in the simple present. When you hear গতকাল (yesterday) you expect the simple past. Learn each time word together with its tense.

কাল (kal) means both 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow'. The tense of the verb tells you which: কাল গেলাম (past) is 'yesterday I went'; কাল যাব (future) is 'tomorrow I will go'. To be clear you can say গতকাল (yesterday) or আগামীকাল (tomorrow).

blocks.title: The same verb with its time word
items: I was eating rice at that time.

blocks.text: Bengali tenses do not match English tenses one for one. Here is how the common English forms are said in Bengali, so you do not translate word for word.

sections.title: Negatives and questions in every tense

The simple past and the present perfect have the same negative: আমি যাইনি means both 'I did not go' and 'I have not gone'. The time word tells you which.

title: বর্তমান কাল
Bortoman kal
The present tenses
blurb: The simple present, the present continuous and the present perfect: when to use each, how to build them, with many examples and the common mistakes.

sections.title: Simple present: habits, facts and routines

blocks.text: The simple present (সাধারণ বর্তমান) is the plainest tense. It is the root plus a person ending, with no tense sign. Use it for three things: habits and routines (what you do regularly), general facts (what is always true), and timetables or fixed arrangements.
Habits and routines

blocks.title: Routines
items: You go to school every day.
He / she reads a book every day.
We walk in the park every day.
He / she listens to a song every day.
What do you do every day?

blocks.text: General facts

blocks.title: Things that are always true
items: The sun rises in the east.
It rains a lot in the monsoon.

blocks.text: Timetables and arrangements

blocks.title: Fixed times
items: The train leaves at eight in the morning.
The shop closes at nine at night.

blocks.text: Negatives and questions

blocks.title: Not and ?
items: He / she does not eat fish.
Do you go to school every day?
We do not go to the market.

blocks.title: Habit or right now?
items: A regular habit (রোজ) needs the simple present, not the continuous.
না comes after the verb, not before it.

blocks.text: The present continuous (ঘটমান বর্তমান) is built with -ছ-: root + ছি / ছিস / ছ / ছেন / ছে. Use it for an action in progress right now, for something temporary around now, and, very commonly, for a plan that is settled for the near future.
Right now

blocks.title: Now
items: He / she is reading a book.
We are listening to a song.
They are playing in the field.

blocks.text: Temporary situations around now

blocks.title: These days
items: This week I am staying in Kolkata.
He / she is studying a lot these days.
We are in a new house now.

blocks.text: A settled plan for the near future
Bengali often uses the present continuous for something you have already decided to do soon. English does the same: 'I am going tomorrow'.

blocks.title: Plans
items: I am going to Kolkata tomorrow.
We are going to school tomorrow.

blocks.text: Negatives and questions

blocks.title: Not and ?
items: I am not eating rice now.
He / she is not reading a book.
Are you listening to a song?

blocks.title: Now needs -ছ
items: খাই sounds like a habit ('I eat'). For an action happening right now, say খাচ্ছি.
For something in progress now use -ছ: করছ. The question word goes before the verb.

sections.title: Present perfect: finished, with a result now

blocks.text: The present perfect (পুরাঘটিত বর্তমান) is built with -েছ-: root + েছি / েছিস / েছ / েছেন / েছে. It is used when an action is finished but is still connected to now: you have eaten (so you are not hungry), you have arrived (so you are here). It is also used for recent events, and for experience.
Done, and it matters now

blocks.title: Finished actions
items: He / she has written a letter.
Father has gone to the office.
He / she has listened to the song.

blocks.text: Experience: have you ever?

blocks.title: Ever and never
items: Have you ever come to Kolkata?
I have never seen a snake.

blocks.text: Not yet
A negative present perfect uses the present form with -নি, and the word এখনও (yet / still) usually goes with it.

blocks.title: Not yet
items: I have not eaten rice yet.
He / she has not come yet.
You have not read the book yet.
We have not written the letter yet.

blocks.text: Bengali uses the present perfect more than English does for recent events. 'I came today' is আমি আজ এসেছি, with the perfect. Use the simple past only when the time is clearly over: আমি গতকাল এলাম.

title: অতীত কাল
Otit kal
The past tenses
blurb: The simple past, the past continuous, the past perfect and the habitual past: what each one says, how to build it, many examples, and how to tell a story in the past.

sections.title: Simple past: it happened, and it is over

blocks.text: The simple past (সাধারণ অতীত) is built with -ল-: root + লাম / লি / লে / লেন / ল. Use it for an action that is finished and sits clearly in the past, usually with a time word that is over: yesterday, last week, in 2010, then. Telling a story, you mostly use the simple past.

blocks.title: Finished actions
items: I went to the market yesterday.
He / she wrote me a letter.
We saw a film on Sunday.
He / she listened to the song.

blocks.text: Not in the past

blocks.title: Negatives and questions
items: I did not go to school yesterday.
He / she did not tell me.
Did you go to the office yesterday?

blocks.title: Yesterday means past
items: গতকাল means yesterday, so the verb must be in the past: গেলাম.
Use the verb form গেলাম, not the dictionary form যাওয়া.

sections.title: Past continuous: in progress at that time

blocks.text: The past continuous (ঘটমান অতীত) is built with -ছিল-: root + ছিলাম / ছিলি / ছিলে / ছিলেন / ছিল. It describes an action that was in progress at a moment in the past, or two things going on together in the background, or an action that was interrupted by another.
In progress at that moment

blocks.title: Then
items: He / she was reading a book then.
We were listening to a song then.
They were playing in the field then.
I was talking on the phone then.

blocks.text: One action interrupted by another
Use যখন … তখন … ('when … then …'). The long action takes the past continuous, and the short action that cut across it takes the simple past.

blocks.title: While and when
items: আমি যখন বাড়ি এলাম তখন সে ঘুমাচ্ছিল।
ami jokhon bari elam tokhon she ghumachchhilo.
When I came home, he / she was sleeping.
আমি যখন খাচ্ছিলাম তখন ফোন বাজল।
ami jokhon khachchhilam tokhon phon bajlo.
When I was eating, the phone rang.
সে যখন পড়ছিল তখন আলো চলে গেল।
she jokhon porchhilo tokhon alo chole gelo.
While he / she was studying, the lights went out.
তুমি যখন এলে আমি রান্না করছিলাম।
tumi jokhon ele ami ranna korchhilam.
When you came, I was cooking.

blocks.text: Not in progress

blocks.title: Negatives and questions
items: I was not eating rice then.
He / she was not sleeping then.
Were you reading a book then?

sections.title: Past perfect: it had already happened

blocks.text: The past perfect (পুরাঘটিত অতীত) is built with -েছিল-: root + েছিলাম / েছিলি / েছিলে / েছিলেন / েছিল. It says that an action had already finished before another moment in the past. It is also the usual way to say that something happened once, a long time ago, and is not connected to now.
Before another past moment

blocks.title: Earlier than another event
items: আমি যখন পৌঁছলাম, সে তখন চলে গিয়েছিল।
ami jokhon pouchholam, she tokhon chole giyechhilo.
When I arrived, he / she had already left.
He / she had already read the book.
We had seen the picture before.
সে আমাকে বলেছিল যে সে আসবে।
she amake bolechhilo je she ashbe.
He / she had told me that he / she would come.

blocks.text: Once, long ago

blocks.title: A past experience
items: Had you come to Kolkata before?
Grandmother lived in this house in her childhood.

blocks.text: Do not confuse the past perfect with the present perfect. আমি খেয়েছি (I have eaten) is about now: you are not hungry. আমি খেয়েছিলাম (I had eaten) is about before something else in the past.

sections.title: Past habitual: what used to happen

blocks.text: The past habitual (নিত্যবৃত্ত অতীত) is built with -ত-: root + তাম / তিস / তে / তেন / ত. It describes what used to happen again and again in the past, and what would happen every time. It is also used for polite or unreal ideas: 'I would say if I knew'.

blocks.title: Used to
items: I used to play in the field every day in my childhood.
What did you use to eat every day?
He / she used to read a book every day.
Grandmother used to tell us stories.
We used to go to the market every Sunday.
Father used to walk every morning.
আমি তখন প্রতিদিন চা খেতাম না।
ami tokhon protidin cha khetam na.
I did not use to drink tea every day then.
Did you use to come here before?

blocks.text: Would, if

blocks.title: Unreal ideas
items: If I had known, I would have said so.
If you had come, I would have been happy.
If I had money, I would buy it.

sections.title: Telling a story: the past tenses together

blocks.text: In a real story the past tenses work together. The simple past moves the story forward. The past continuous paints the background. The past perfect looks back to what had already happened. The habitual says what used to be true. Read the example, and notice which tense each sentence uses.

Yesterday morning I woke up.  (simple past: the story moves)
Mother was cooking then.  (past continuous: background)
Father had already gone to the office.  (past perfect: earlier)
I washed my face and drank tea.  (simple past)
In my childhood I used to walk to school.  (habitual past)
Today I went to school by bus.  (simple past)

title: ভবিষ্যৎ কাল
Bhobishyot kal
The future tenses
blurb: The simple future, the future continuous, other ways to talk about what comes next, 'if … then', and 'has been doing for'.

blocks.text: The simple future (সাধারণ ভবিষ্যৎ) is built with -ব-: root + ব / বি / বে / বেন / বে. It is used for what will happen, for promises and decisions, for predictions, and for polite requests (with আপনি as a question).
Plans and promises

blocks.title: Will
items: I will go to the market tomorrow.
We will see a film tomorrow.
I will write you a letter.

blocks.text: Not in the future

blocks.title: Negatives and questions
items: He / she will not eat rice.
We will not go to school tomorrow.

blocks.text: Polite requests with the future

blocks.title: Please
items: Will you give me a little water? (polite)
Will you help me a little? (polite)
Will you sit here a little? (polite)

blocks.text: The future continuous (ঘটমান ভবিষ্যৎ) says what will be in progress at a time in the future. It is built from the -তে form plus থাকব: root + তে থাকব / থাকবি / থাকবে / থাকবেন / থাকবে. It is found in textbooks and in careful writing. In everyday speech people more often use the simple future or say 'I will be doing' with a different word order.

blocks.title: Will be doing
items: আমি কাল সকালে বই পড়তে থাকব।
ami kal shokale boi porte thakbo.
I will be reading a book tomorrow morning.
He / she will be working in the evening.
আমরা ওই সময় বাড়িতে থাকতে থাকব।
amra oi shomoy barite thakte thakbo.
We will be staying at home at that time.

blocks.text: Say 'কাল সকালে আমি বই পড়ব' (I will read a book tomorrow morning) in conversation. Use the continuous form when you want to stress that the action will still be going on.

sections.title: Other ways to talk about the future

blocks.text: Bengali has several everyday ways to speak about the future besides the simple future tense.

blocks.title: 1. A settled plan: present continuous
blocks.text: When a plan is already fixed, use the present continuous, as English does.
items: I am going to Kolkata tomorrow.

blocks.title: 2. Wanting: -তে চাই
blocks.text: To say what you want or intend to do, use the -তে form of the verb with চাই.
items: He / she wants to be a doctor.

blocks.title: 3. Thinking of doing: -ব ভাবছি
blocks.text: To say you are thinking of doing something, use the future form followed by ভাবছি.
items: I am thinking of going tomorrow.
We are thinking of buying a house.

blocks.title: 4. Being about to: -তে যাচ্ছি
blocks.text: To say something is about to happen, use the -তে form with যাচ্ছি.
items: I am about to eat now.
It is about to start raining.

blocks.title: 5. Having to: -তে হবে
blocks.text: To say you must or will have to, use the -তে form with হবে.
items: I will have to work tomorrow.

blocks.text: For a possible event in the future, the 'if' part takes the -লে form and the 'then' part takes the future tense: যদি তুমি এসো আমি যাব, or simply তুমি এলে আমি যাব. The word যদি (if) may be added, and তাহলে (then) can start the second part.

blocks.title: Possible conditions
items: If you come, I will be happy.
If it rains, we will not go.
যদি তুমি পড়ো তাহলে পাশ করবে।
jodi tumi poro tahole pash korbe.
If you study, then you will pass.
If you ask, I will do it for you.
If I get money, I will buy a house.
If you feel cold, put on a shirt.
If I have time, I will come.
তুমি না এলে আমি যাব না।
tumi na ele ami jabo na.
If you do not come, I will not go.

blocks.text: English says 'I have been learning Bengali for two years'. Bengali does not use a special tense for this. It uses the present continuous with ধরে (for) or থেকে (since). The action is still going on, so the verb stays in the continuous.

head: Word
Meaning

rows: a length of time: দুই বছর ধরে

blocks.title: For and since
items: আমি দুই বছর ধরে বাংলা শিখছি।
ami dui bochhor dhore bangla shikhchhi.

title: কারক
Karak
Karak: the job of each noun
blurb: Every noun in a sentence does a job for the verb. Learn the six jobs (doer, receiver, tool, beneficiary, source, place) and how to find each one by asking the verb a question.

blocks.text: কারক (karak) is the relationship between a noun or pronoun and the verb of the sentence. The verb is the centre of the sentence, and every noun connected to it does one of six jobs. Learning to see these jobs makes a long sentence easy to read and helps you choose the right ending for each noun.

The easiest way to find a noun's karak is to ask the verb a question. Ask 'Who does it?', 'What is it done to?', 'With what?', 'For whom?', 'From where?', 'Where or when?'. The noun that answers the question is that karak.

head: Karak
Job
Question you ask the verb
Example (the karak is underlined in the meaning)
rows: what or whom the action is done to
the one given to or for
কাকে? কার জন্য? (to whom? for whom?)
কোথা থেকে? কার কাছ থেকে? (from where?)

blocks.text: Two more relationships appear in sentences but are not counted among the six karaks in most school grammars: সম্বন্ধ (belonging, like 'of') and সম্বোধন (calling someone by name). They are explained in the last section.
Reading a sentence with karaks
Take one sentence with several jobs: রাহুল কলম দিয়ে বন্ধুকে চিঠি লিখল (Rahul wrote a letter to his friend with a pen). Ask the verb লিখল each question in turn.

blocks.title: How to find the karaks in any sentence
items: Find the verb: it is usually the last word.
Ask কে? The answer is the কর্তা.
Ask কী? or কাকে? The answer is the কর্ম.
Ask কী দিয়ে? The answer is the করণ.
Ask কার জন্য? or কাকে? (for a gift). The answer is the সম্প্রদান.
Ask কোথা থেকে? The answer is the অপাদান.
Ask কোথায়? or কখন? The answer is the অধিকরণ.

blocks.text: The কর্তা (kortha) is the doer, the person or thing that does the action. Ask the verb কে? (who?). In most sentences the কর্তা comes first. It takes no ending in the usual sentence: রাম যায় (Ram goes).

blocks.title: Finding the doer
blocks.text: Ask 'Who does the verb?'. The answer is the কর্তা, whatever the tense and whatever the other words are.
items: Who reads? সে is the doer.

blocks.title: The doer in a sentence
items: Father goes to the office. (কর্তা: বাবা)
They play in the field. (কর্তা: তারা)
Brother will write a letter. (কর্তা: ভাই)

blocks.text: The doer can have an ending
Three common shapes of the doer: plain (রাম), with -রা for a group of people (ছেলেরা), and with -ই for emphasis (সে-ই করেছে, 'it was he who did it').

blocks.title: Plain, plural, emphatic
items: The boys are playing in the field.
It was he who called me.

blocks.text: The doer of a feeling: in the possessive
With verbs of feeling, the one who feels takes the possessive: আমার খিদে পেয়েছে, 'hunger has come to me'. The person is still the doer in meaning, even though the form is আমার.

blocks.title: The doer takes no -কে
items: The doer takes no -কে. -কে marks the receiver of an action.

sections.title: কর্ম: what the action is done to

blocks.text: The কর্ম (korma) is the object: what or whom the action is done to. Ask the verb কী? (what?) or কাকে? (whom?). A person or an animal that is a কর্ম usually takes -কে; a thing usually takes no ending.

blocks.title: Two kinds of কর্ম
blocks.text: মুখ্য কর্ম (the main object) is usually a thing; গৌণ কর্ম (the secondary object) is the person who receives it. In 'I gave the boy a book', the book is the main object (বই) and the boy is the secondary object (ছেলেটিকে).
items: I gave the boy a book.  বই: main; ছেলেটিকে: secondary.

blocks.text: Things: no ending
People and animals: -কে
Two objects in one sentence

blocks.title: Person and thing
items: Father gave me a book.  আমাকে: person; বই: thing.
The teacher told the students a story.
He / she wrote me a letter.

blocks.text: A thing can take -কে too, when it is definite and being singled out: আমি বইটাকে ভালোবাসি, 'I love that book'. But the plain thing without -কে is the usual form.

blocks.title: -কে for people, not for things
items: A thing as an ordinary object takes no ending.
A person as the object takes -কে.

blocks.text: The করণ (koron) is the tool, instrument or means by which the action is done. Ask the verb কী দিয়ে? (with what?) or কীসে? The words দিয়ে and দ্বারা show it, and sometimes the ending -এ / -য়.

blocks.title: Ways to mark the tool
blocks.text: দিয়ে comes after the noun in speech: কলম দিয়ে (with a pen). দ্বারা is the formal word. -এ or -য় can be joined to the noun: হাতে (with the hand), চোখে (with the eye), ট্রেনে (by train).

blocks.title: With what?
items: He / she cuts fruit with a knife.
We eat rice with a spoon.
He / she opened the lock with a key.
Mother washed her hands with water.

blocks.text: The vehicle or means of travel

blocks.title: By what?
items: He / she goes to school by bus.
We crossed the river by boat.

blocks.text: দিয়ে is also used with people to mean 'through, by means of': আমি তাকে দিয়ে কাজ করালাম, 'I had the work done by him'. It is more advanced; for now learn the tool sense.

The সম্প্রদান (sampradan) is the one to whom something is given freely, or for whom something is done. Ask the verb কাকে? (to whom?) or কার জন্য? (for whom?). The marker is -কে, or জন্য placed after the possessive form.

blocks.title: Marking the receiver
blocks.text: Use -কে for a person who is given something: ভিখারিকে ভিক্ষা দিলাম. Use জন্য for the person or thing something is done for: মায়ের জন্য ফুল আনলাম.
items: I gave food to the poor man.

blocks.title: Given to, done for
items: I gave food to the poor man.
Mother gave milk to the baby.
I gave my friend a gift.
বাবা আমার জন্য একটা বই আনলেন।
baba amar jonyo ekta boi anlen.
Father brought a book for me.
He / she gives to the poor.
We gave money for the school.

blocks.text: The same word can be কর্ম or সম্প্রদান: in 'আমি রামকে দেখলাম' (I saw Ram), রামকে is the object of seeing (কর্ম). In 'আমি রামকে বই দিলাম' (I gave Ram a book), রামকে is the receiver (সম্প্রদান). Ask the verb: dekha gets 'whom?', dena gets 'to whom?'.

The অপাদান (apadan) is the place or person something comes from, moves away from, or is separated from. Ask the verb কোথা থেকে? (from where?) or কার কাছ থেকে? (from whom?). The marker is থেকে after the noun.

blocks.title: Marking the source
blocks.text: Put থেকে after the noun: বাড়ি থেকে (from the house). For a person, use -র কাছ থেকে: বন্ধুর কাছ থেকে (from a friend).

blocks.title: From where? From whom?
items: The river comes down from the hills.
আমি বন্ধুর কাছ থেকে বই নিলাম।
ami bondhur kachh theke boi nilam.
I took a book from a friend.
সে মায়ের কাছ থেকে টাকা পেল।
she mayer kachh theke taka pelo.
He / she got money from his / her mother.
He / she came out of the room.

blocks.text: Cause and comparison
You also say who you learn from with -র কাছ থেকে, and fear is said with -কে: আমি সাপকে ভয় পাই. Comparison with চেয়ে is covered in the lesson on bibhakti.

blocks.title: Other uses
items: আমি শিক্ষকের কাছ থেকে বাংলা শিখি।
ami shikkhoker kachh theke bangla shikhi.
I learn Bengali from the teacher.

sections.title: অধিকরণ: the place and the time

blocks.text: The অধিকরণ (adhikoron) tells where or when the action happens. Ask the verb কোথায়? (where?) or কখন? (when?). The usual marker is -এ after a consonant, -তে after a vowel, and -য় after -া.
Where

blocks.text: When

blocks.title: Time
items: He / she goes to the park in the afternoon.
I drink tea in the morning.

blocks.text: In a state or condition

blocks.title: Condition
items: I am in joy (I am happy).
He / she is shaking with anger.

sections.title: Putting it together: reading whole sentences

blocks.text: Now find every karak in a full sentence. Work through the questions one at a time. Each noun gets exactly one job.

blocks.text: Two more relationships appear in sentences. School grammars usually do not count them among the six, because they do not connect to the verb directly.

blocks.title: সম্বন্ধ (sombondho): belonging
blocks.text: The relation between two nouns: whose is it? The first noun takes -র / -এর: রামের বই (Ram's book), আমার বাড়ি (my house). It answers কার? (whose?).

blocks.title: সম্বোধন (sombodhon): calling someone
blocks.text: The name or word you use to call someone. It is not part of the verb's work. It often comes first and takes no ending: রাম, এসো! (Ram, come!).

title: বিভক্তি
Bibhakti
Bibhakti: case endings and little words
blurb: The seven bibhaktis: the endings and small words that go after a noun to show its karak. How each one is formed, when to use it, and what the little words after nouns mean.

blocks.text: বিভক্তি (bibhakti) is the ending or small word that is added to a noun or pronoun to show what job it does in the sentence. The job is called the কারক (karak), and the ending that shows it is the বিভক্তি. Karak is the role; bibhakti is how the role is written.

Traditional grammar counts seven bibhaktis, named by number: প্রথমা (first), দ্বিতীয়া (second), তৃতীয়া (third), চতুর্থী (fourth), পঞ্চমী (fifth), ষষ্ঠী (sixth), সপ্তমী (seventh). Here they are with the markers each one uses.
The names and the exact grouping differ a little between textbooks. Some books combine the second and fourth, because both use -কে. Follow your teacher's table when it differs from this one.
Karak and bibhakti side by side

sections.title: How the endings attach to a noun

blocks.text: The ending you add depends on how the noun ends. Learn the three groups: nouns that end in a consonant, nouns that end in a vowel sign (-ি, -ী, -ু, -ে), and nouns that end in -া. A few common words are irregular, and they are listed in the table.

blocks.title: Rules of thumb
items: After a consonant, the 'of' ending is -এর: ঘর → ঘরের. After a vowel sign or -া it is -র: বাড়ি → বাড়ির, রাস্তা → রাস্তার.
The 'in' ending is -এ after a consonant (ঘরে), -তে after a vowel sign (বাড়িতে), and -য় after -া (রাস্তায়).
Words that end in the vowel ই, like বই and দই, add -য়ের: বই → বইয়ের.
Persons take -কে for the object. Things usually take no ending.
থেকে is a separate word and never changes the noun: ঘর থেকে.
For a person, the source is -র কাছ থেকে: বন্ধুর কাছ থেকে (from a friend).

blocks.text: Places rarely take -কে (the object ending), and people rarely take the locative -এ / -তে. That is why the table leaves those cells empty.

The first bibhakti (প্রথমা, nominative) marks the doer (কর্তা). It usually has no ending at all. The doer just stands in front of the verb. You can add -রা to a group of people, -ই for emphasis, or -টা / -টি for 'the'.

blocks.title: No ending on the doer
items: The boys are playing in the field.
It was he who did this.
The book is on the table.

blocks.text: The second bibhakti (দ্বিতীয়া, objective) marks the object (কর্ম). People and animals take -কে. Things take no ending, unless you single out one definite thing (বইটাকে).

blocks.title: -কে for people
items: I am listening to this song.

blocks.title: Use the object form of pronouns
items: The pronoun needs its object form: তোমাকে.

blocks.text: The third bibhakti (তৃতীয়া, instrumental) marks the tool or means (করণ). It uses দিয়ে after the noun, or the ending -এ / -য়, or the formal word দ্বারা.

blocks.title: With what?
items: He / she eats with the hand.
Mother cut the fruit with a knife.
He / she opened the door with a key.
He / she wrote with a pen. (formal)
He / she washed the hands with soap.

blocks.text: The fourth bibhakti (চতুর্থী, dative) marks the one to whom something is given or for whom it is done (সম্প্রদান). It uses -কে for the receiver, and জন্য after the possessive for 'for'. In many books it overlaps with the second bibhakti, since both can use -কে.

blocks.title: To and for
items: I gave a book to my friend.
Mother gave milk to the baby.
I gave money to the poor man.
Father brought a shirt for me.
আমরা সবার জন্য খাবার রান্না করলাম।
amra shobar jonyo khabar ranna korlam.
He / she bought medicine for his / her mother.

blocks.text: The fifth bibhakti (পঞ্চমী, ablative) marks the source or the starting point (অপাদান). It uses থেকে after the noun, and also হতে in writing. It marks comparison too, with চেয়ে after the possessive form.

blocks.title: From
items: A fruit fell from the tree.
আমি বন্ধুর কাছ থেকে বই পেলাম।
ami bondhur kachh theke boi pelam.
I got a book from a friend.
সে আজ সকাল থেকে কাজ করছে।
she aj shokal theke kaj korchhe.
He / she has been working since this morning.
Delhi is very far from Kolkata.

blocks.text: Comparison: চেয়ে
To say 'more than', put the thing compared after the possessive form and then চেয়ে (than). The adjective follows.

blocks.title: More than
items: আমার চেয়ে সে ভালো গাইতে পারে।
amar cheye she bhalo gaite pare.
He / she can sing better than I.

blocks.text: The sixth bibhakti (ষষ্ঠী, genitive) shows belonging or relation, like English 'of' or '’s'. It ends in -র after a vowel (বাড়ির) and -এর after a consonant (ঘরের). The possessive pronouns (আমার, তোমার, তার) are genitives too. The owner comes before the thing owned.

blocks.title: Whose?
items: My friend's house is in Kolkata.
The door of the room is open.
What is the price of the book?
The teachers of our school are good.
His / her brother's name is Rahul.

blocks.text: A chain of belonging

blocks.title: One after another
items: The roof of my friend's house.
The name of the teacher's daughter's book.

blocks.text: With the ending -র/-এর, the owner changes and the thing owned stays the same. With আমার, the same form works for 'my' with every noun: আমার বই, আমার ঘর, আমার বন্ধুরা.

The seventh bibhakti (সপ্তমী, locative) marks the place or the time (অধিকরণ): where something happens or when. The ending is -এ after a consonant, -তে after a vowel, and -য় after -া. It also marks a state or condition.

blocks.title: Where, when, in what state
items: He / she is in the room.
They are walking on the road.
The book is on the table.
The bird is sitting on the tree.
I drink tea in the morning.

blocks.text: Words that work like 'in' and 'on'
For more precise places, a possessive noun plus a position word is used: ঘরের ভিতরে (inside the room), টেবিলের উপর (on the table). See the next section.

Where English puts a preposition before the noun ('on the table'), Bengali puts a small word after it ('table on'). These are called অনুসর্গ (onushorgo), postpositions. Some of them take the genitive (-র / -এর) before them. Others follow the plain noun.

blocks.title: In sentences
items: The book is on the table.
The cat is sitting under the tree.
He / she is inside the room.
I saw a film with a friend.
There is a shop in front of the school.
He / she went out without an umbrella.
তার মতো গান কেউ গাইতে পারে না।
tar moto gan keu gaite pare na.
Nobody can sing like him / her.

blocks.title: Genitive or plain?
items: Words like উপর, নিচে and সঙ্গে need the genitive -র / -এর before them.
থেকে follows the plain noun, with no -র.

blocks.text: The plural endings and the case endings can be combined. The plural -রা marks the doer. The ending -দের covers both the object and 'of' for people: ছেলেদের means 'the boys' (object) and 'of the boys' (genitive). For things, add -গুলো first and then the case ending: বইগুলোর (of the books), বইগুলোতে (in the books).

blocks.title: Plurals and endings
items: The boys are playing in the field.
The boys' books are on the table.
The price of the books is high.
We listened to the girls' song.

title: বচন
Bochon
Number: one, many and counting
blurb: Singular and plural: how to say 'a', 'the' and 'some', how to make plurals for people and for things, and how to count with the right counting word.

blocks.text: Bengali has two numbers. একবচন (ekbochon) is singular and বহুবচন (bohubochon) is plural. Four rules are enough for a first lesson.

blocks.title: After a number, no plural marker
blocks.text: When you count, the noun stays singular and a counter follows the number: -টা (-টো, -টে) for things and -জন for people.

sections.title: One or many: singular and plural

blocks.text: বচন (bochon) means 'number': one or many. Singular is একবচন (ek-bochon, 'one-number') and plural is বহুবচন (bohu-bochon, 'many-number'). Bengali treats number more lightly than English. A plain noun can mean one or many, and the plural ending is used only when you need to be clear. The verb never changes for number.
The same noun, one and many

blocks.title: One and many
items: I have many books. (a plain noun after 'many')
The book is on the table. (one, known)
The books are on the table. (many, known)

blocks.text: The verb stays the same: ছেলেটি পড়ছে (one boy is studying) and ছেলেরা পড়ছে (the boys are studying) both use পড়ছে. Only the noun, and the pronoun, show number: আমি → আমরা, সে → তারা.

Bengali has no separate words for 'a' and 'the'. Instead it uses small endings on the noun, together with one (এক). A plain noun is general: বই (a book, books). To say 'one book' use একটা বই or একটি বই. To say 'the book' add -টা (spoken) or -টি (written, formal) to the noun: বইটা, বইটি.

blocks.text: Bengali has several plural endings, and the choice depends on whether the noun is a person or a thing. For people use -রা (or -েরা after some words). For things and animals use -গুলো (or the literary -গুলি). In writing you also meet -সমূহ, -বৃন্দ and -গণ for formal groups.
Plural of people

items: The boys are playing in the field.

blocks.text: Plural of things and animals

blocks.title: -গুলো
items: The books are on the table.
The birds are sitting on the tree.
The shirts have to be washed.

blocks.text: Singular and plural pairs

blocks.title: People or things?
items: For people, -রা is the natural plural. -গুলো is for things, or used for people only with a slightly negative tone.

blocks.text: When you count things, Bengali puts a counting word (a classifier) after the number: দুটো বই 'two-ish book', পাঁচজন ছাত্র 'five-person student'. Use -টা (or -টি) for things and animals, and -জন for people. After a number the noun stays singular: it never takes -গুলো.
Counting things

blocks.title: -টা
items: There are four chairs at the table.
Ten birds are sitting on the tree.

blocks.text: Counting people

blocks.title: -জন
items: There are five students in the class.
How many of you are there?

blocks.text: Units and measures
For quantities of food and drink, use the measure word the way English does: a cup of tea, a kilo of potatoes. There is no counting word, because the measure is the counting word.

blocks.title: Measures
items: Please give one cup of tea.
I bought a kilo of potatoes.
I ate a plate of rice.
We will need two litres of milk.

blocks.title: Counting rules
items: After a number the noun stays singular. Do not add -গুলো.

sections.title: A, the and some: the same noun four ways

blocks.text: Put together everything about singular and plural, and you can say four different things about one noun. Compare them side by side.
Words for quantity
Words like অনেক (many, much), কিছু (some), সব (all), কয়েকটা (a few), একটু (a little) stand in front of a plain noun with no plural ending.

blocks.title: Quantity words

প্রত্যেক ছেলে একটা করে বই পেল।

blocks.text: Only the pronoun shows number in Bengali, never the verb. Each singular pronoun has a plural partner: আমি → আমরা, তুমি → তোমরা, আপনি → আপনারা, সে → তারা. The verb after the plural pronoun is exactly the same as the one after the singular.

title: লিঙ্গ
Ling
Gender: he, she and it
blurb: Gender in Bengali lives only in some nouns. Learn the pairs, the two common endings, and the big surprise: he and she, verbs and adjectives do not change.

blocks.text: লিঙ্গ (ling) means 'gender'. Bengali has three kinds. পুংলিঙ্গ (pumlingo) is masculine, স্ত্রীলিঙ্গ (strilingo) is feminine, and ক্লীবলিঙ্গ (klibolingo) is neuter, for things with no gender. You only need to remember the three terms once: the important thing is how gender behaves.

In Bengali, gender shows only in the words themselves. A few nouns have a masculine and a feminine form, like ছেলে (boy) and মেয়ে (girl). Everything else in the sentence stays the same. This is much simpler than languages where verbs and adjectives change for gender.
Many words for people come in pairs. Learn them together.
In sentences

sections.title: Two endings that make the feminine

blocks.text: Many pairs follow a pattern. Some feminine words are made by changing the ending of the masculine word. Others are separate words, so learn them one by one.
Many people today use the masculine form for both, for example শিক্ষক for any teacher. The feminine forms are still correct and you will hear and read them often.
This is the good news. In Bengali the pronoun সে, the verb and the adjective stay the same for men and women.

blocks.title: Do not change the adjective
items: The adjective does not take a feminine form. ভালো is used for girls and boys alike.

blocks.text: Some words are for both men and women: ডাক্তার (daktar, doctor) is used for a male or a female doctor, and so are বন্ধু (friend), মানুষ (person) and শিশু (child). Things such as বই (book), টেবিল (table) and গাছ (tree) are neuter: they take no gender at all.

items: My friend is a doctor. (a man or a woman)

blurb: Negatives (না, নি, নয়, নেই), yes/no questions, every question word, and how to answer.

blocks.text: To make a verb negative, Bengali adds a small word after it. In most tenses the word is না. In the simple past and the present perfect it is the ending -নি, joined to the verb. The verb itself keeps its person ending, so you can still tell who is acting.

blocks.text: Bengali has four everyday words for 'not', and each does a different job. Choosing the right one is mostly a matter of what kind of sentence you have.

Used for

Meaning

blocks.text: নেই covers the present only. In the past and the future, the negative of আছে is ছিল না and থাকবে না.

Bengali builds words like 'nobody', 'nothing', 'nowhere' and 'never' from a question word plus a small word, and then makes the verb negative as well. Two negatives do not cancel each other. They agree.

items: I have never seen a snake.

blocks.text: To ask a question that can be answered 'yes' or 'no', add কি (or কী) to the sentence, usually after the first word or just before the verb. In speech you can also keep the same sentence and raise your voice at the end. The word order does not change.

blocks.title: Making a yes/no question
blocks.text: Put কি into the statement, or raise your voice at the end. The rest of the sentence stays the same.

items: Does he / she stay at home?
Did you go to the office yesterday?

blocks.text: Questions with just a rising voice
Either … or …
To ask a choice, put বা or না between the two parts. 'Or' is বা, অথবা or কিংবা in writing; in speech you often hear না.

items: Will you have tea or coffee?

Will you go by bus or by train?

blocks.text: Checking: …, তাই না?

blocks.title: Tag questions
items: You will come tomorrow, won't you?

blocks.text: Question words usually sit just before the verb, where the answer would sit. They are called প্রশ্নবাচক শব্দ. Learn them as a set, because you will use them in every conversation.
Who, what, where
When, why, how
How much, how many, which, whose

blocks.title: কত, কয়টা, কোন, কার

blocks.text: The usual answer to a yes/no question is the verb, said again, or হ্যাঁ (yes) or না (no). Bengali does not need a pronoun in the answer. For a question word, answer with just the missing piece.

Building sentences
blurb: Word order, describing words, comparing, joining sentences with 'and', 'but' and 'because', and giving reasons.

blocks.text: A Bengali sentence usually follows the order subject – object – verb (SOV): আমি ভাত খাই, literally 'I rice eat'. The verb comes last. English puts the verb in the middle (subject – verb – object), so this is the first big habit to learn.

blocks.title: The order of a plain sentence
blocks.text: Doer first, then the other parts (time, place, object), and the verb at the very end.
items: He / she reads a book. (he – book – reads)

blocks.title: A fuller sentence: আমি রোজ সকালে বাজারে মাছ কিনি
head: Part
Position
Example

blocks.title: Verb last
items: আমি রোজ সকালে বাজারে মাছ কিনি।
ami roj shokale bajare mach kini.
I buy fish at the market every morning.
Mother is cooking rice in the kitchen.
The teacher told the students a story in class.
He / she will write a letter to a friend tomorrow.
We play in the park on Sundays.
I did not have tea this morning.
The boys are playing football in the field.

blocks.title: Do not put the verb in the middle
items: The verb goes at the end.

blocks.text: In speech, and in poetry, a word is sometimes moved to the end for stress: খাই আমি ভাত? is rare, but আমি যাব না, কাল is a natural afterthought. As a learner, keep to subject – object – verb.

An adjective (বিশেষণ) comes before the noun it describes: ভালো বই (good book), বড় বাড়ি (big house). An adverb (ক্রিয়াবিশেষণ) comes before the verb it describes: আস্তে বলো (speak slowly). Adjectives do not change for number or gender, and the noun carries any ending.
Adjectives before nouns

blocks.title: Describing nouns
items: He / she is wearing a new shirt.

blocks.text: An adjective after the noun, as the answer
When the adjective says what something is, it often comes at the end of the sentence without a verb: ঘরটা বড় (the room is big).
Adverbs: how, how much
To compare, put the thing you compare with in the genitive (-র / -এর) and add চেয়ে (than). The adjective stays as it is. To say 'the most', use সবচেয়ে or সবার চেয়ে (more than all).

blocks.title: More than, as … as, the most
items: He / she is as tall as I am.
He / she is the best student in the class.
This is the most beautiful picture.

sections.title: Joining sentences: and, but, or, so

blocks.text: Short words join one idea to another. Learn the most common ones, and you will be able to build sentences of any length.

blocks.text: And, but, or

blocks.title: Joining equals
items: আমি চা খাই আর সে কফি খায়।
ami cha khai ar she kophi khay.
I drink tea and he / she drinks coffee.
আমি বাজারে গেলাম এবং মাছ কিনলাম।
ami bajare gelam ebong mach kinlam.
I went to the market and bought fish.
আমি যাব, কিন্তু সে যাবে না।
ami jabo, kintu she jabe na.
I will go, but he / she will not.
Will you have tea or coffee?
Ram and Shyam are two friends.

blocks.text: Reasons: কারণ and তাই
Both words say that one thing is the reason for another. তাই comes after the reason and introduces the result. কারণ comes after the result and introduces the reason.

blocks.title: Because and so
items: I am tired, so I will sleep.
আমি যাব না, কারণ বৃষ্টি হচ্ছে।
ami jabo na, karon brishti hochchhe.
I will not go, because it is raining.
তার জ্বর হয়েছে, তাই সে আসেনি।
tar jor hoyechhe, tai she asheni.
He / she has a fever, so he / she did not come.
সে আসেনি, কারণ তার জ্বর হয়েছে।
she asheni, karon tar jor hoyechhe.
He / she did not come, because he / she has a fever.
আমার খিদে পেয়েছে, তাই আমি খাচ্ছি।
amar khide peyechhe, tai ami khachchhi.
I am hungry, so I am eating.
It is raining, so take an umbrella.

blocks.text: When, if, that

blocks.title: Longer sentences
items: যখন বৃষ্টি পড়ে তখন আমি বাড়িতে থাকি।
jokhon brishti pore tokhon ami barite thaki.
When it rains I stay at home.
যদি তুমি আসো তাহলে আমি খুশি হব।
jodi tumi asho tahole ami khushi hobo.
If you come, then I will be happy.
সে বলল যে সে কাল আসবে।
she bollo je she kal ashbe.
He / she said that he / she will come tomorrow.
আমি জানি যে তুমি ভালো আছ।
ami jani je tumi bhalo achho.
I know that you are well.
তাড়াতাড়ি চলো, না হলে দেরি হবে।
taratari cholo, na hole deri hobe.
Hurry up, otherwise we will be late.

sections.title: How much, how many: quantity words

blocks.text: Quantity words stand before a noun and usually need no plural ending: অনেক বন্ধু (many friends), কিছু জল (some water).

blocks.title: Quantity words in sentences
items: All the students are in class.

sections.title: Building a long sentence step by step

blocks.text: You can build a long, natural sentence by adding one piece at a time. Start with the core and add time, place, description and reason, always keeping the verb last.

blocks.title: Growing a sentence
items: Add a place: আমি বাজারে যাই। (I go to the market.)
Add a time: আমি রোজ বাজারে যাই। (I go to the market every day.)
Add the object: আমি রোজ বাজারে মাছ কিনতে যাই। (I go to the market every day to buy fish.)
Add a description: আমি রোজ সকালে বাজারে তাজা মাছ কিনতে যাই। (I go to the market every morning to buy fresh fish.)
Add the reason: আমি রোজ সকালে বাজারে তাজা মাছ কিনতে যাই, কারণ বাড়িতে মাছ ছাড়া ভাত হয় না। (… because rice without fish is not a meal at home.)
